newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: Why women are wading into the Web.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: Why women are wading into the Web.

text.p: The chance of women networking with other women on the Internet was fairly infrequent not so long ago.
Indeed one of the hazards of joining Internet chat rooms was that they were usually dominated by men.
But that is changing rapidly as more women discover the power and freedom of the new digital world.
Forrester Research has forecast that by the year 2000, some 18 million U.S. women will be on the Internet, up from about five million now.
There have been all kinds of reasons given why men have gravitated to computers and the Web much faster than women, with many explanations vaguely insulting to both sides of the gender divide.
The usual rationale is that men tend to be enamored with "toys," while women have an aversion to dealing with complicated gadgets.

For many, personal computers are the muscle cars of the 1990s. Some techies are often more keen to talk about the power under their hoods -- the ram, the rom, the bits and bytes -- than what the machines actually do for them in practical terms.
Many industry leaders believe a sign of maturity of the Internet and computing in general wil be when users reach the point where they talk more about where the automobile goes than what powers it.

The influx of women on the Web may be a sign that the medium has progressed to the realm of the useful. A number of women have put up a range of sites just for women, while other groups have launched pages with the idea of attracting readership from both sexes.
Boots Co Plc said in July it launched a site aimed mainly at women. Boots estimated that of the 1.8 million Internet users in the United Kingdom, some 540,000 were women.
"Boots has designed its site with the consumer and particularly the 18-34-year-old female customer in mind," said Gary Cormack, head of marketing services at Britain's largest pharmacy company.
The page offers such things as a vitamin database, weather maps and beauty chat and fathers' chat forums.

WomenZone (www.cybergrrl.com) has become a hugely popular site for female surfers in the United States and elsewhere. The area has a cyber magazine covering health issues, a search engine for women-related Internet sites and Webgrrls, an international networking tool.
In Canada last Wednesday, a not-for-profit group launched CoolWomen (www.coolwomen.org) to celebrate and promote the development of women in Canadian society.

"Over the past year, a group of us met over endless lasagna to talk about what we wanted to create: stories of women and girls, readily accessible, and about how to do this in every country on the planet," said Nancy Ruth, one of the founders, at the launch of the site.
Cool Women offers browsers the chance to contact other women at the site through "fe/mail" and other features such as the "Cool Woman of the Week" and a bulletin board for upcoming events.
Beth Atcheson, project manager for CoolWomen, said that the group found in designing the site that women were just discovering what the Web could do for them -- and were pleasantly surprised.

She found that women had been heavy users of e-mail, but had not quickly adopted the technology needed for the Web. But as they discovered the medium, they tended to stay at a site longer, rather than hop to every hyperlink that came along.
"Women tend to use the Internet a little differently," said Atcheson.
